Finding a doctor on Medicare

People on Medicare and their families struggle to keep a doctor or find one who will take them.

“Without any notice from UHC, they cancelled our Primary Care Physician from their network effective 3/31/2026”, a member of a Medicare Advantage plan wrote on a forum in March 2026.

We read 53 accounts that people on Medicare, their families and doctors' offices gave in public. They come from forums, news stories, hearings and advocacy groups. Forty-two are from people on Medicare and their families. Most of them had lost a doctor, or could not find one who would take them. For many, the practice did not take their kind of Medicare. Fewer got a wrong answer about whether a doctor was in their plan. CMS is building a national directory of doctors. Accurate listings in it could help with the wrong answers. It could also say which kind of Medicare a practice takes new patients on. We would test first whether people would then make fewer calls.

Where people look today

In these accounts, more people couldn't keep or find a doctor than got a wrong answer.

Of these 42 people, 32 lost a doctor or could not find one who would take them. For 14 of them, the practice did not take their kind of Medicare. Others had a doctor who would not see them, or who left their plan while they were in care. Some had no doctor nearby in their plan. Nine got a wrong or conflicting answer about whether a doctor was in a plan. Five of them had both problems.

Most often, people asked a doctor's office or their insurance company. Few called Medicare or used its website.

Some went without care. A woman of 73 with two stage 4 cancers had found a therapist to help with end-of-life issues. When the therapist left her plan's network, she could not afford the higher rates and stopped seeing her therapist. A retiree in Mississippi stopped going to the doctor because she could not pay out of pocket.

When CMS checked Medicare Advantage directories between June 2022 and June 2024, it found that “44.29 percent of the location listings in the online provider directories contained at least one inaccuracy”. It gave that figure in its proposed rule of October 2026.

Losing a doctor

A doctor leaves someone's plan, or won't see them at all.

Some people were in care when their doctor, or their hospital and its doctors, left their Medicare Advantage plan. For others, the doctor took no new Medicare patients, or saw only people 65 or older. Some called office after office to find a doctor who would take them.

One. One called back
A 60-year-old Colorado man with a disability. After his endocrinologist dropped his Medicare patients, he contacted 31 doctors. He finally found a new endocrinologist (2012).

What happened to them

Dropped from the network, no notice

A couple joined a Medicare Advantage plan on January 1, 2026. Their primary care doctor was dropped from its network as of March 31. They found out less than two weeks before the doctor left. By then, only days were left to change Medicare Advantage plans.

We received no notice of this change, but rather had to find out by going on line and logging into our account
A member, on an AARP forum (2026)

Rural, and stopped going

A retiree in rural Holly Springs, Mississippi, had gone to the local hospital and clinic for decades. Her new Medicare Advantage plan did not cover them, and they were the only care within 25 miles. She could pay out of pocket or drive out of town to a doctor she didn't know. She went back to Original Medicare with a supplement, and to her regular doctor.

I didn't go to the doctor because I was going to have to pay out-of-pocket money I didn't have.
Told to NBC News (2023)

Under 65, on disability

A person under 65 was on Medicare because of a disability. Their primary care doctor began seeing only people 65 or older. They called every office their plan covered and could not find another.

I cannot see specialists I need without a primary care's referral!
A person in New Mexico, on a forum (2022)

Turning 65

A woman had seen the same therapist for about six years. Medicare did not pay marriage and family therapists like hers until January 2024. She waited six months to see a social worker who took Medicare.

About six months before I turned 65, she told me that she was not going to be able to see me anymore because of the fact that I was going to be on Medicare.
A woman whose job is helping seniors find mental health services, on NPR (2024)

The Colorado man got a letter saying his endocrinologist would stop seeing him and other Medicare patients. When a woman in Washington, D.C., turned 65, her internist didn't take Medicare patients. It took her 18 months to find a new doctor. A forum poster believed their office was dropping them “because they don't want to take my Medicare anymore.” In Vancouver, Washington, a large clinic chain saw people on almost any Medicare Advantage plan. People on Original Medicare could see its specialists, but could not have a primary care doctor there. Someone replying in the comments gave a reason: such groups are in “a financial risk-sharing arrangement with Medicare Advantage plans.” In these four accounts, the person knew the doctor would not take them. None of them got a wrong answer.

Joan · new to Medicare

Joan's plan lists her doctor, but the doctor's office says it isn't in her network.

Joan is a composite. Her age, the year, her start date and where she enrolled are made up. The other steps happened to real people who joined a Medicare Advantage plan because their doctor was listed.

I joined Medicare Advantage when I became eligible for Medicare a few months ago because my doctor was listed as a participating provider.
A letter to AARP Bulletin's Medicare column (2026)

From the accounts

When we started, my primary care provider was listed so I went ahead and applied. I got a confirmation letter.
Someone choosing a plan with their wife, on an AARP forum (2020)

From the accounts

The day my coverage began, I attempted to make an appointment with the physician, but was told by the insurance billing office that none of the physicians in their office is in the network!
A letter to PBS NewsHour's Medicare column (2017)

From the accounts

I spoke with a customer service representative from the MA plan and explained the inaccurate, discrepant information in its online directory.
The same letter (2017)

From a news story

CMS gives most Advantage members two chances to change plans: during the annual open enrollment period in the fall and from January until March 31.
KFF Health News (2024)

From CMS

This SEP is only open to people who relied on incorrect information from Plan Finder (not from a plan website).
CMS fact sheet, March 2026. SEP is short for special election period.

Joan turns 65 in spring 2026. She finds her doctor in an insurance company's online directory. She joins its Medicare Advantage plan on the company's website. Her Medicare and her plan both start on April 1.

On April 1 she calls her doctor's office to book a visit. The billing office tells her none of its doctors are in her plan's network.

She calls the insurance company and explains that its online directory is wrong.

She looks for a way to change plans. Most people on Medicare Advantage get two chances a year, in the fall and from January to March 31. The next one is not until the fall.

For 2026, CMS opened an extra chance to change plans, called a special election period. It is for people who relied on wrong information in Plan Finder. Joan joined on the insurance company's website, so she does not qualify. If she had joined through Plan Finder and it had listed her doctor wrongly, she could have switched. She would have had to call 1-800-MEDICARE within her first 3 months on the plan.

Joan writes to an advice column to ask whether she can switch plans. Others have asked the same question. One person wrote to PBS NewsHour's Medicare column in 2017, after finding their listed doctor was out of network. Another wrote to AARP Bulletin's Medicare column in 2026.

Under CMS's rules, Joan can change plans once, until the end of June, her third month on Medicare. She joined at 65, so she can also switch to Original Medicare any time in her first year on the plan. The counselor who answered the AARP letter did not mention either option. We can't tell from either letter whether those options applied, or what happened next.

Elena · caring for her father

Elena gets different answers on whether her father's specialist is in his network.

Elena is a composite too, drawn from two families' accounts from 2015 and 2026. Her father is on a Medicare Advantage plan, and she handles his care.

From the accounts

He still thinks he has Medicare primary and UnitedHealthcare as a secondary insurance.
An adult child writing about their father, in Physicians Practice (2015)

From the accounts

A physician listed as in-network one day was listed as out-of-network the next.
Families USA, on a son's calls to his mother's insurance company (2026)

From the accounts

At check-in, the registration desk informed them the visit would be billed as out-of-network.
Families USA, on the same son and his mother (2026)

From the accounts

if there isn't a physician that fits the requirements of Dad's care, they would have to provide the authorization to see an out-of-network physician, as that was not Dad's problem they didn't fill up their network.
The adult child, on a call with their father's medical group (2015)

From the accounts

A few hours later poof! They found a doctor only 10 minutes from his house that was just credentialed that day.
The same adult child (2015)

Elena's father thinks he has Medicare, with a second insurance on top. In fact he is on a Medicare Advantage plan. To see a specialist, he needs a referral from his primary care doctor.

His doctor refers him to a specialist. Elena calls his insurance company to check that the specialist is in its network. She gets different answers on different calls.

On one call the company says yes, so she drives him an hour and a half to the appointment. At check-in, the desk says the visit will be billed as out of network. The scan the specialist orders is out of network too. It would cost about $3,000.

She gets her father and his medical group on one call. If the group has no specialist he can see, she says, it has to approve one outside the network.

A few hours later the group finds a specialist 10 minutes from his house. The specialist had joined its network that day.

In Families USA's 2026 story, the son spent hundreds of hours on the phone. His mother started cancer treatment seven months after he first took her to the emergency room. She died three months later. Families USA calls it “many failures, across many systems, over many years”. The writer of the 2015 article works in medical billing, and wrote about their father:

there is no way he would ever have been able to get this figured out without my help.
The adult child, on their father (2015)

Doctors' offices

Offices send the same details to every plan they work with, in the format that plan asks for.

Insurance companies list doctors partly from what offices send them. Dr. Jack Resneck Jr., president of the American Medical Association, spoke to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2023. He said practices typically work with 20 or more plans. He works at a large university hospital with a big staff for this work. Even so, he said, plans usually take 6 to 8 months to add or remove a doctor after the hospital tells them.

The offices' accounts are mostly about insurance plans in general. Only two are about Medicare Advantage plans. We found no account from someone who works at a front desk.

They do not use standardized formats, so we have to send different rosters with different formatting to each and every one.
Dr. Jack Resneck Jr., to the Senate Finance Committee (2023)

From the offices

17 forms, every 90 days

A social worker in California runs a group practice. Since a state law on directories passed, her insurance companies send her a form every 90 days to confirm her listing. Filling them all out takes about a day, unpaid. If she misses one, that insurer could drop her from its directory.

I have 17 insurance contracts. I have to fill out 17 attestations
Told to the California Health Report (2021). An attestation is a form confirming a listing.

Listed as the wrong kind of doctor

A neurologist in a one-doctor office is listed as a psychiatrist. No insurance company has asked him to check his listing.

No, I'm not a psychiatrist. And no one's asked me.
In Texas Medicine (2023)

What one doctor would rather have

Patients told a Texas neurologist that his insurer had dropped him from its network. Nothing had lapsed, and the insurer could not say why. He would rather get an email from insurers, with a link to log in and check his listing.

In an ideal world, I would say it's an email
In Texas Medicine (2023)

The National Provider Directory

CMS is building a national directory of doctors. A record in it shows a doctor's Medicare status.

CMS means the National Provider Directory to be “the authoritative public-facing platform for provider directory information”. On November 20, 2026, it was a preview site at directory.cms.gov. Its help pages say it suits people who need detailed provider data. They send people on Medicare to Care Compare.

If Joan looked up her doctor in the national directory today, she would see Medicare marked “Participating”. It would not say whether the doctor is in her Medicare Advantage plan. The directory's help pages say that plan information is coming. Someone on a Medicare Advantage plan might read “Participating” as a yes. We would test whether they do.

Medicare.gov's Plan Finder does show which doctors are in a plan's network. For 2026, CMS bought those lists from a vendor, as a short-term step. CMS warns that “some provider directory information may be incorrect, especially in this first year”. For 2027 plans, the insurance companies were due to send CMS their lists, starting October 1, 2026. CMS says Plan Finder will later use the national directory's data.

CMS expects insurance companies' network lists to feed the national directory one day. Then it could help people get the right answer about whether a doctor is in their plan. It cannot make a doctor take someone, or keep a network from changing. The American Medical Association warned senators that “a bloated provider directory may be hiding a network that is wholly inadequate to serve the needs of the plan's enrollees”. The directory could also say which kind of Medicare a practice takes new patients on. The redrawn record gives a single “Yes” to “Accepting new patients”.

The National Provider Directory (NPD) is in preview release.

What we would test first

We would start with five questions, and test them with people on Medicare, their families, counselors and doctors' offices.

  1. Would people make fewer calls if a directory showed which kind of Medicare a practice takes new patients on?

    Test with people on Original Medicare and on Medicare Advantage plans who are looking for a doctor, and with office managers at one-doctor offices and large groups.

  2. When a doctor or hospital leaves a plan, how and when do people find out? What do they believe they can do?

    Test with people on Medicare Advantage plans in the middle of care with a doctor, SHIP counselors, and family members who make the calls.

  3. Before joining a plan, how do people check that their doctors are in it? What do they take as the answer?

    Test with people choosing or changing a Medicare Advantage plan, including people new to Medicare, and family members who make the calls.

  4. When a record says a doctor participates in Medicare, do people on a Medicare Advantage plan think the doctor is in their plan?

    Test with people on Medicare Advantage plans and on Original Medicare, side by side.

  5. How would an office like to check and correct its listing?

    A form from every plan, a fax, an email with a link, or a doctor signing in to the directory. Test with doctors, practice owners and front-desk staff, from one-doctor offices to large centers.

I'm sticking with her because she knows everything about me
A woman in Durham, North Carolina, on her doctor. A SHIP counselor helped her change plans before the December 7 enrollment deadline, so she could keep the doctor (2023).

Prepared by Focus Consulting, November 2026. AI helped find the 53 accounts, from 2008 to 2026. A script checked every quote against a saved copy of its source.

An AI model tagged all 451 quotes with problems from a fixed list. It found 32 accounts about a doctor people can't keep or find, and 9 about a wrong answer. A second model, working without the first one's results, found 30 and 8. A researcher then checked 5 of the tags behind the counts, drawn at random. Four held up. The fifth was moved from the wrong-answer count to the can't-keep-or-find count.

Joan and Elena are composites of real, cited accounts. Private people are described by their role, not their name. The sources are listed on a separate page.
